# Sakuṇagghijātaka (Ja 168)

**ID:** Ja 168
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Sakuṇagghijātaka

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sakuṇagghijātaka* (Ja 168) is a canonical birth story situated in the *Dukanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana in connection with his teaching in the *Sakuṇovādasutta* (found in the *Satipaṭṭhāna-saṁyutta* of the *Saṁyutta Nikāya*, SN 47.6), wherein he admonished the monks to wander within their own home territory and ancestral realm (*gocare bhikkhave caratha sake pettike visaye*) [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. As Oskar von Hinüber observes, the prose text of the *Sakuṇagghijātaka* is drawn directly from this *Saṁyutta Nikāya* sutta [von Hinüber 1994].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a quail (*lāpa*), whose ancestral territory is a clod of earth in a plowed field, while Devadatta represents his adversary, a hawk or falcon (*sakuṇagghi* / *sena*) [Bodhi 2003; Fausböll 1879; von Hinüber 1994]. Straying beyond his own domain into foreign feeding grounds, the quail is captured by the bird of prey [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. The quail laments that had he remained in his ancestral realm, the hawk could not have defeated him [Fausböll 1879]. Overconfident in its own power, the hawk releases the quail and challenges him to fight on the quail's home ground; when the hawk swoops forcefully down upon him (*seno balasā patamāno*), the quail nimbly retreats into the clod of earth at the last moment, causing the hawk to strike the ground with full force and perish [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879; von Hinüber 1994]. Linguistically, the narrative preserves archaic grammatical forms, notably the reduplicated aorist *ajjhapattā* / *ajjhapatto* [Bodhi 2003; von Hinüber 1994].
